passage: Ganga, you asked why I volunteer at the hospice every Saturday. It started after my mother. She was ill for four years, and I was the one who sat with her at night, learning how to lift her, how to hold her hand when the pain came. When she died, I felt empty and useless. Six months later I walked into the hospice and asked if they needed anyone. Now I read to patients and sit with families. I'm Darshan, and it has given my loss a purpose. But I'll be honest: last month a woman there hummed my mother's song, and I had to leave and cry in the car park. The work doesn't replace the grief. I've started seeing a grief counsellor too. Both need space.

qa.q: How long was Darshan's mother ill?
qa.a: Four years.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel after the mother died?
qa.a: Empty and useless, before finding purpose at the hospice.

qa.q: What balance is Darshan learning?
qa.a: Keeping the caring work for purpose, while also giving grief its own space, by crying when it comes and seeing a grief counsellor.

qa.q: What might the families at the hospice experience with Darshan?
qa.a: Comfort from someone who understands long illness, who sits with them and reads to patients.

grounding: An adult who lost a parent to a long illness volunteers at a hospice, finding purpose while still needing to grieve.

passage:
January: Six months after his father's death from a long lung illness, Manoj quits his sales job and enrols in a nursing course. "I learned so much in those hospital nights," he tells his friend Tenzin. "I want to use it."
April: Manoj is top of his class in patient care. He works double shifts on the training ward and never talks about his father. Tenzin notices he hasn't taken a day off since January.
July: On the anniversary of his father's death, Manoj freezes by a patient's bed when the man coughs the same way. He goes into the staff room and sobs. His supervisor sits with him. That evening he calls Tenzin: "I think I've been working instead of grieving." They light a lamp together for his father.

qa.q: What course did Manoj enrol in?
qa.a: A nursing course.

qa.q: What did Manoj feel when the patient coughed like his father?
qa.a: He froze and then sobbed; the grief he had been working through instead of feeling came flooding back.

qa.q: What does Manoj realise, and what might help?
qa.a: That he has been working instead of grieving; keeping the nursing purpose while taking time off and marking the loss, as with the lamp, gives grief its own space.

qa.q: What had Tenzin noticed by April?
qa.a: That Manoj hadn't taken a day off since January, which worried Tenzin.

grounding: An adult who lost his father to a long illness trains as a nurse, and learns his grief also needs its own space.

passage: Bidisha, you ask why I started the kitchen at the cancer hospital. When I was twenty-five, your Gurleen masi lost her mother after three long years of illness. In those years I had seen families sleeping in the corridor, eating only biscuits. After Bibiji died, I couldn't sit at home. So I began cooking dal and rotis and taking them to the hospital every Sunday. Soon others joined. It gave my grief somewhere to go. But I'll tell you the part people skip: two years in, I realised I had never cried for Bibiji. I was always too busy feeding others. One Sunday I stayed home, took out her shawl, and wept all day. Service is a good home for grief, beta. It is not the only room.

qa.q: What did Gurleen cook for the hospital?
qa.a: Dal and rotis.

qa.q: What did young Gurleen realise two years in, and how did she feel?
qa.a: That she had never cried for Bibiji; the grief she had been too busy to feel came through, and she wept all day.

qa.q: What choice in the story gave grief its own room?
qa.a: Staying home one Sunday with Bibiji's shawl to weep, instead of only serving others.

qa.q: How might the families in the corridor have experienced the kitchen?
qa.a: As real comfort, a warm meal instead of only biscuits during a hard time.

grounding: An elder recalls turning grief for her mother into a hospital kitchen, and learning the grief still needed its own space.

passage: The power went off during the monsoon reading lesson, and Ramesh sir asked Sarika to read aloud by the light from the window. She stumbled on "environment", then on "enormous". A boy at the back snickered. Quick as anything, Sarika crossed her eyes, puffed out her cheeks and said in a robot voice, "Sarika has stopped working! Please restart!" The class burst out laughing, with her this time. Ramesh sir smiled too. But at break he noticed Sarika sitting alone, picking at her tiffin. "That was funny," he said. "Is reading aloud hard for you?" She shrugged, then nodded, very small. "Every time." He said they could practise together at lunch, just the two of them.

qa.q: Which two words did Sarika stumble on?
qa.a: "Environment" and "enormous".

qa.q: Why did Sarika do the robot act?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed after stumbling and hearing the snicker; the joke let her control the moment so the class laughed with her, not at her.

qa.q: What did Ramesh sir do that was wise?
qa.a: He noticed her alone at break, looked past the joke to ask whether reading aloud was hard, and offered private practice.

qa.q: How might the boy who snickered feel after the joke?
qa.a: He probably laughed along; the moment turned, and his snicker lost its sting.

grounding: A girl who stumbles while reading gets the class laughing with her, and a teacher sees the worry behind the clowning.

passage: In the week before Durga Puja, the Kolkata school buzzed with holiday plans. When Sumit's turn came to read the Bengali poem aloud, he tripped over a long word and his face went red. Then he stood up straight, bowed like a king, and said, "Thank you, thank you, I'll be here all week." Everyone laughed. The teacher shook her head, smiling. Sumit did it every time now: a joke, a face, a bow. His friend Sharmila noticed he never read more than two lines before joking. Walking home past the bamboo of the half-built pandal, she asked, "Do you joke because reading is hard?" Sumit kicked a pebble. "If they laugh at the joke, they don't laugh at me," he said.

qa.q: What did Sumit say after bowing?
qa.a: "Thank you, thank you, I'll be here all week."

qa.q: Why does Sumit joke every time he reads?
qa.a: He feels embarrassed and worried about stumbling, and the joke keeps control, so they laugh at the joke and not at him.

qa.q: What could help Sumit beyond the jokes?
qa.a: Telling the teacher or a parent that reading aloud is hard, so he gets practice and support instead of always hiding it.

qa.q: What has Sharmila noticed?
qa.a: That Sumit never reads more than two lines before joking, so she senses the worry behind it.

grounding: A boy who stumbles reading aloud turns it into a joke every time, and a friend sees the worry it hides.

passage:
"How was school, Lavanya?"
"Great, Amma! I made the whole class laugh."
"Oh? How?"
"I was reading about the planets and I said a name wrong, so I pretended to be an alien. Everyone laughed."
"With you or at you?"
"With me. Because I did it first."
Her mother, Sharmila, put down the knife. "Do you do that a lot?"
"Kind of. Whenever I read."
"What happens if you don't make a joke?"
Lavanya went quiet. "Then they might laugh the other way."
"That sounds tiring, chellam."
"It is," Lavanya whispered. "Sometimes."
"Shall we read together tonight, under the winter blanket? No audience."
"Okay."

qa.q: What did Lavanya pretend to be?
qa.a: An alien.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's reply about them laughing the other way reveal?
qa.a: She is worried about being laughed at, and joking first protects her; it also makes her tired.

qa.q: What did Sharmila suggest?
qa.a: Reading together tonight under the blanket, with no audience, so Lavanya can practise without needing a joke.

qa.q: How might Sharmila feel on learning Lavanya jokes every time she reads?
qa.a: Concerned and tender, sensing how tiring it is for her daughter.

grounding: A girl who stumbles when reading clowns so the class laughs with her, and her mother sees the worry beneath.

passage: When I got braces in Class 9, I decided to strike first. "Metal mouth reporting for duty!" I'd say before anyone else could. I called myself "tin can" and "robot jaws". It worked; people laughed with me, and nobody got the chance to be mean. But after a few months I noticed something. The boys at the back had started calling me "tin can" too, and not kindly. They had learned it from me. One day my friend Joseph said, "You're funny, Sabina, but you're always the joke." That stung. So I stopped. It was scary at first, just smiling with my braces and saying nothing. But the nickname faded. I'm still funny. I just don't aim at myself every time.

qa.q: Which names did Sabina joke with about the braces?
qa.a: "Metal mouth", "tin can" and "robot jaws".

qa.q: How did Sabina feel when Joseph said "you're always the joke"?
qa.a: It stung; Sabina felt hurt and exposed, realising the self-mockery had taught others to aim at Sabina.

qa.q: What did Sabina change, and what happened?
qa.a: Sabina stopped the self-mocking jokes, even though it felt scary, and the nickname faded.

qa.q: How did the boys at the back respond to Sabina's jokes over time?
qa.a: They picked up "tin can" and used it unkindly, learning to see Sabina as a target.

grounding: A teenager mocked their own braces first to win acceptance, until the self-mockery taught others to treat them as a target.

passage: Class teacher's note, Term 1. Kavitha has a habit of announcing her own low marks before anyone else sees them: "Drumroll... another proud 12 out of 40 from the class genius!" The class laughs, and she smiles. But this week I heard Preeti's friends call her "class genius" in a mean way, and Kavitha laughed along with her eyes down. I think the jokes began as protection and are now teaching others how to treat her. I spoke with Kavitha privately. She said, "If I say it first, it hurts less." We agreed she will try a week without the jokes, and I will check in with her daily. I will also talk to the group about the nickname.

qa.q: What mark did Kavitha announce?
qa.a: 12 out of 40.

qa.q: Why does Kavitha announce her own low marks?
qa.a: She feels embarrassed and worried about being mocked, and saying it first hurts less.

qa.q: What plan did the teacher and Kavitha agree on?
qa.a: A week without the self-mocking jokes, daily check-ins, and the teacher talking to the group about the nickname.

qa.q: How have Preeti's friends picked up on Kavitha's jokes?
qa.a: They now use "class genius" meanly, having learned from her jokes that she is a target.

grounding: A teenager mocks her own marks before others can, which wins laughs but teaches others to target her.

passage:
Friday.
Did my usual bit in class today. When the maths results came back, I held mine up and said, "Another masterpiece from the family failure!" Everyone laughed. Even Anirban laughed, and he never laughs. It felt good for about ten seconds. Then at lunch, someone at the next table said, "Ask the family failure, she won't mind." And I did mind. I minded a lot. I think I've been teaching them the joke. If I keep calling myself stupid, why wouldn't they? Tomorrow I'm going to try just taking my paper and saying nothing. That's going to be harder than any joke.
Payal

qa.q: What did Payal call herself in class?
qa.a: "The family failure."

qa.q: How did Payal feel when someone used the nickname at lunch?
qa.a: Hurt; Payal minded a lot, even though the joke had felt good for about ten seconds in class.

qa.q: What is Payal planning, and why?
qa.a: To take the paper and say nothing tomorrow, because the self-mockery was teaching others to mock her.

qa.q: How might Anirban have seen Payal's joke?
qa.a: As genuinely funny, since he rarely laughs, without realising it hurts her underneath.

grounding: A teenager mocks her own marks first, and realises the joke is teaching others to target her.

passage: Noor, you asked for a disaster story? The night before our final robotics demo, our robot, Chintu, drove straight off the table and into a bucket of mop water. Just drove into it, like it had given up on life. There were four of us, it was 2 a.m., and nobody said anything for a second. Then Jahnavi, that's me, started laughing. Then everyone was laughing, the kind where you can't breathe. Someone said, "Chintu chose peace." It was awful and hilarious. And after ten minutes of that, we were calmer. We dried the board, made a list, split the tasks, and rebuilt the motor by eight. The demo worked. I don't think we'd have managed it if we'd started with panic.

qa.q: What did the robot drive into?
qa.a: A bucket of mop water.

qa.q: How did the team feel once the laughing had passed?
qa.a: Calmer and less tense; laughing at the absurdity together gave them relief and some distance from the shock.

qa.q: What did the team do after laughing?
qa.a: They dried the board, made a list, split the tasks, and rebuilt the motor by eight.

qa.q: What would have changed if they had started with panic?
qa.a: They might have blamed each other or frozen, and might not have rebuilt in time.

grounding: Students whose project crashes laugh at the absurdity, then calmly plan and fix it.

passage: I'm the lab assistant in the media building, so I saw the whole thing. At midnight the hard drive holding Himani and Pradeep's group film clicked twice and died. Three weeks of footage. For a moment they just stared. Then Pradeep said, very seriously, "Well. It was a silent film anyway," and Himani laughed so hard she sat on the floor. They all laughed, a bit wildly. I thought they had lost it. But then Himani stood up, wiped her eyes, and said, "Okay. What do we still have?" They found phone backups and a rough cut in someone's email. By 2 a.m. they had a plan on the whiteboard. I can't say what they felt inside, but the laughing didn't stop the work. It started it.

qa.q: How much footage was on the hard drive?
qa.a: Three weeks of footage.

qa.q: What might the group have felt when the drive died?
qa.a: Shock and dismay at first, then a wild relief in laughing at the absurdity.

qa.q: What did the group do right after laughing?
qa.a: Asked "What do we still have?", found phone backups and a rough cut, and had a plan on the whiteboard by 2 a.m.

qa.q: How did the lab assistant see the laughter at first, and later?
qa.a: At first the narrator thought they had lost it; later saw that the laughing started the work.

grounding: An observer watches students laugh at a failed hard drive, then turn to planning.

passage:
Tuesday night: Yogesh and Vishal's team discover their survey app has been saving every answer as "banana". Two hundred responses, all "banana". They stare at the screen. Then Vishal reads aloud, in a newsreader's voice, "Question twelve: how satisfied are you with the canteen? Banana." The whole team collapses laughing.
Wednesday: Still grinning, they work out what went wrong: a test value left in the code. They split the jobs: fix the bug, draft a polite message, contact the class groups again.
Saturday: A hundred and forty new responses are in, real ones. At the team meeting, someone brings bananas. They laugh again, then get back to the analysis.

qa.q: How many responses had been saved as "banana"?
qa.a: Two hundred.

qa.q: How did the team feel when Vishal read "Banana" aloud?
qa.a: They went from stunned dismay to helpless laughter, which eased the shock.

qa.q: What did they do after the laugh?
qa.a: Found the cause, a test value left in the code, split the jobs, fixed the bug, and contacted the class groups again.

qa.q: How might the classmates asked to answer again feel?
qa.a: Perhaps mildly annoyed, but the polite message helped, and 140 of them responded.

grounding: A student team laughs at an absurd bug that ruined their survey, then plans and fixes it.

passage: Himani, you know our friend Aakash, the funniest person in any room? Last month I started noticing something. I'm Devika, and I'm nosy, I admit. Whenever anyone asked him a real question, like "How's your dad doing?" or "Are you okay after the layoffs?", he'd crack a joke and change the subject. Every single time. Everyone laughed; he's brilliant. But one evening, after the group left, I saw him sitting alone in the car park, not on his phone, just staring. So the next day I messaged him privately: "You're hilarious. And you can also not be hilarious with me, any time." He didn't reply for an hour. Then he wrote, "Dad's not doing well." We talked for two hours.

qa.q: Where did Devika see Aakash sitting alone?
qa.a: In the car park.

qa.q: What did Devika feel seeing Aakash alone in the car park?
qa.a: Worried and tender, sensing pain behind his constant jokes.

qa.q: Why did Devika's private message work?
qa.a: It praised his humour while giving him permission not to be funny, in private, so he could share about his dad.

qa.q: What was Aakash carrying under the jokes?
qa.a: Worry about his father's health, which he finally shared.

grounding: A friend notices the funniest person dodging serious questions with jokes and checks in privately.

passage: I've shared a desk with Vinita at the design studio for a year, and she's the reason our team lunches are fun. Last week, during a serious talk about burnout, someone asked her directly, "Vinita, how are you finding the workload?" She did her famous impression of our manager and everyone laughed. Then she did it again when her mother's surgery came up. I'm Kunal, and I'm not good at feelings, but I noticed she never answers those questions. Not once. I can't know what's going on for her. So I didn't push at the table. I left a sticky note on her monitor: "Chai at four? No jokes required." She came. She was quiet for a while, then said, "I'm really tired, Kunal."

qa.q: What did Kunal write on the sticky note?
qa.a: "Chai at four? No jokes required."

qa.q: What did Kunal feel noticing Vinita's pattern?
qa.a: Concerned and unsure; Kunal didn't know what was going on but sensed something behind the jokes.

qa.q: Why didn't Kunal push at the table?
qa.a: A public question would likely get another joke; a private, low-pressure invitation made room for honesty.

qa.q: What did Vinita admit over chai?
qa.a: That she is really tired, something her jokes had been covering.

grounding: An observer notices a funny colleague deflecting every serious question with a joke and checks in privately.

passage:
Friday: At the college reunion dinner, Rajni keeps everyone in stitches. When Alka asks how her new job is going, Rajni says, "Oh, amazing, I'm basically the CEO now," and launches into a story about a pigeon in the office. Everyone laughs. Alka notices the job question never got an answer.
Sunday: In the group chat, someone asks Rajni about moving cities. She sends a meme. Alka feels a small worry settle in her chest.
Tuesday: Alka calls Rajni directly, when nobody else is around. "I love your jokes. I also noticed you didn't answer about the job. How is it, really?" There's a long pause. Then Rajni says, "Horrible. I cry in the lift." Alka listens. Before they hang up, she offers to visit on Saturday.

qa.q: What did Rajni tell a story about?
qa.a: A pigeon in the office.

qa.q: What did Alka feel after the meme in the group chat?
qa.a: A small worry settling in her chest.

qa.q: How did Alka check in wisely?
qa.a: She called privately, praised the jokes, gently named the unanswered question, then listened and offered to visit.

qa.q: What was Rajni hiding behind the jokes?
qa.a: That the new job is horrible and she cries in the lift.

grounding: A friend notices someone always answers serious questions with jokes and checks in privately when the joking stops.

subtype: Joke used to dodge a real conversation [Receiver]
passage: The rent was due tomorrow, the landlord had already messaged twice, and the power had just gone out. By candlelight, Pema tried again. "Urmila, we need to talk about money. The credit card bill, the rent." Urmila grinned. "Money? Never heard of it. Is it a fruit?" Pema laughed despite herself, then tried again. "I'm serious." Urmila put on a newsreader's voice. "Breaking news: local couple discovers candles." Pema stopped laughing. She felt the old sinking feeling of talking to a wall made of jokes. "When you joke every time," she said quietly, "I feel like it's only my problem." Urmila's smile faded. The candle hissed. "Okay," Urmila said at last. "No jokes. Tell me."

qa.q: What did Urmila ask about money?
qa.a: "Is it a fruit?"

qa.q: How did Pema feel after the second joke?
qa.a: She felt the old sinking feeling, dismissed, as if talking to a wall made of jokes and as if the problem were only hers.

qa.q: What helped Pema get through?
qa.a: Saying calmly how the jokes made her feel, like it's only her problem, which let Urmila drop the jokes and listen.

qa.q: What might Urmila have been feeling behind the jokes?
qa.a: Possibly anxious or embarrassed about money, using humour to avoid the worry.

grounding: A partner trying to talk about money keeps getting witty deflections and feels dismissed, until she names the feeling.

subtype: Joke used to dodge a real conversation [Receiver]
passage: On the balcony of their small Mumbai flat, Nandini opened the notebook where she tracked their spending. "Vijay, can we look at this together? We keep running short by the twentieth." Vijay clutched his chest. "The twentieth! Our mortal enemy!" She smiled a little. "Seriously." "Seriously, I propose we move to a cave. No rent. Only bats." Nandini closed the notebook. It was the third time this month. Every time she raised money, he made her laugh, and every time the problem stayed in her lap. She felt dismissed and alone with it. "I love your jokes," she said. "But right now they feel like a door closing." Vijay went still. "Okay," he said. "Show me the notebook."

qa.q: By which date do they keep running short?
qa.a: The twentieth.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel after the cave joke?
qa.a: Dismissed and alone with the problem, since it was the third time that month.

qa.q: What did Nandini say that changed things?
qa.a: That she loves his jokes but right now they feel like a door closing, naming the effect without attacking him.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel when Nandini says it?
qa.a: Surprised and sobered, going still, then willing to look at the notebook.

grounding: A partner trying to discuss money keeps meeting witty deflections and feels dismissed, then names it.

subtype: Joke used to dodge a real conversation [Receiver]
passage:
"Irfan, the electricity bill came. It's double."
"Double? Our fridge must be secretly running a factory."
"Ha. But really, we need a plan."
"I have a plan. We become candle people. Very romantic."
"Irfan."
"Or we unplug the fridge and eat everything tonight. A feast!"
Tarun didn't laugh this time. "Every time I bring up money, you make a joke. I end up feeling like the nag, and you get to be the fun one."
Irfan's grin slipped. "I didn't know it felt like that."
"It does. I need you to be serious for ten minutes."
Irfan sat down. "Okay. Ten minutes. Show me the bill."

qa.q: How much had the electricity bill gone up?
qa.a: It was double.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel about the repeated jokes?
qa.a: Dismissed, and cast as the nag while Irfan got to be the fun one.

qa.q: What did Tarun ask for, and why did it work?
qa.a: Ten serious minutes, after saying clearly how the jokes felt, which let Irfan drop the humour.

qa.q: How did Irfan react when Tarun named it?
qa.a: Irfan's grin slipped; Irfan hadn't realised how it felt, and agreed to look at the bill.

grounding: A partner who wants to talk about money keeps hearing jokes, feels dismissed, and asks for ten serious minutes.

subtype: Friend all good then all bad [Actor]
passage: Jeevan, don't even say her name to me. Last week I told you Isha was the best friend anyone ever had. Perfect. She shared her notes, she walked me home, she laughed at every joke. And then yesterday she sat with the new girl at lunch. Didn't even save my seat! So now I know. She was fake all along. A traitor. I'm Vidya, and I don't forgive traitors. ...Wait, why are you looking at me like that? ...Okay, fine. Maybe "traitor" is a lot. She did bring me soup when I was sick last month. I just... it felt like she chose someone else. It felt huge. Maybe it was just one lunch.

qa.q: What did Isha do yesterday?
qa.a: She sat with the new girl at lunch and didn't save Vidya's seat.

qa.q: Why does Vidya call Isha a traitor?
qa.a: Vidya felt hurt and left out when Isha sat with the new girl, and the strong feeling made it hard to remember the good sides.

qa.q: What could help Vidya see Isha more fully?
qa.a: Pausing to recall the good things, like the soup, and telling Isha about feeling left out instead of deciding she was fake.

qa.q: How might Isha feel if she hears she's a traitor?
qa.a: Shocked and hurt, since she was probably just being kind to a new girl.

grounding: A teenager who called a friend perfect last week calls her a traitor after one small slight, then starts to soften.

subtype: Friend all good then all bad [Actor]
passage:
Monday: Zubin tells his mother that Bhavna is "the most loyal friend in the universe" because she lent him her calculator.
Thursday: Bhavna forgets to invite Zubin to the study group. Zubin comes home furious. "She's a snake. She was never my friend. I'm blocking her." His mother asks, "The same Bhavna from Monday?" "She was fake on Monday too."
Saturday: Bhavna messages: "So sorry, I thought Kavya had added you! Come on Sunday?" Zubin stares at it. He remembers the calculator, the notes she shared before the maths test. He feels confused. She isn't a snake. She isn't perfect either. She's just Bhavna. He types, "ok, see you Sunday."

qa.q: What did Bhavna lend Zubin on Monday?
qa.a: Her calculator.

qa.q: How does Zubin feel reading Bhavna's message?
qa.a: Confused, as his all-bad picture of her clashes with the calculator and the shared notes; she is neither a snake nor perfect.

qa.q: What helped Zubin hold both sides?
qa.a: Bhavna's apology and his memories of her kindness; his mother's question also hinted that one slight doesn't erase the good.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt when she realised Zubin wasn't added?
qa.a: Sorry and keen to fix it, messaging to invite him on Sunday.

grounding: A teenager swings from calling a friend perfect to calling her a snake after one slight, then begins to hold both sides.

subtype: Friend all good then all bad [Actor]
passage: Mohit, you're calling Arun your enemy now? Last month he was your hero. Let me tell you about your Swati bua at fourteen. I had a friend, Lata, who was everything to me. I told everyone she was perfect. Then one day she laughed when the teacher scolded me, just a small laugh. I decided she was the worst person alive. For two weeks I wouldn't look at her. Then my mother asked, "Was she perfect before, or just kind to you?" I thought about it. She was kind. And she had laughed that once, unkindly. Both were true. The day I understood that, I went and sat next to her again. We're still friends, beta. Sixty years.

qa.q: What did Lata do that upset young Swati?
qa.a: She laughed when the teacher scolded Swati.

qa.q: Why did young Swati decide Lata was the worst person alive?
qa.a: She felt hurt and betrayed by the small laugh, and the strong feeling made it hard to hold on to Lata's good sides.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Her mother's question, "Was she perfect before, or just kind to you?", which helped her hold both truths.

qa.q: How might Lata have felt during those two weeks?
qa.a: Confused and hurt, perhaps not even knowing why Swati had stopped looking at her.

grounding: An elder recalls idealising a friend and then seeing her as all bad after one slight, until she learned to hold both.

passage:
"Professor Iyer is a genius, Farhan. The best teacher in this entire university. Maybe in India."
"He's good, yeah."
Two weeks later:
"Professor Iyer is a fraud, Farhan. Did you see what he wrote on my draft? 'Lazy argument.' Lazy! After everything."
"You were quoting him every day last week."
"That was before I saw who he really is."
"Thomas. One comment."
"One comment that tells you everything."
"Or one comment on one draft. Was it lazy?"
Thomas paused. "The third section was a bit rushed."
"So he's a good teacher who said one harsh thing."
"...I put him really high up, didn't I?"
"Like, on the moon, man."

qa.q: What did Professor Iyer write on Thomas's draft?
qa.a: "Lazy argument."

qa.q: Why does Thomas now call the professor a fraud?
qa.a: He felt stung and let down by the harsh comment, and because he had put the professor so high, one flaw made the whole picture collapse.

qa.q: How did Farhan help Thomas?
qa.a: He asked whether the draft was lazy, helping Thomas see the professor as a good teacher who said one harsh thing.

qa.q: How might Professor Iyer see the comment?
qa.a: As ordinary feedback on a rushed section, probably unaware of how deeply it hurt.

grounding: A student who idolised a professor turns bitter after one harsh comment, until a friend helps him see an ordinary flaw.

passage: In my second year, I thought Dr Menon was the wisest person alive. I copied her way of writing, almost her handwriting. I told everyone I wanted to be exactly like her. Then, at my first conference, she introduced another student's poster and walked past mine without a word. That evening I told my friend Darshan she was arrogant, cold, overrated. I skipped her next two lectures. Darshan asked, "Did she promise to see your poster?" She hadn't. She had been running the whole session. I had built her so high that when she turned out to be a busy human, I felt robbed. I went back to her class. She's still brilliant. She also forgets posters. I'm Gargi, and I've learned to admire people without worshipping them.

qa.q: How many of Dr Menon's lectures did Gargi skip?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: Why did Gargi feel robbed when Dr Menon walked past the poster?
qa.a: Gargi had built her up so high that an ordinary moment of busyness felt like betrayal, turning admiration into bitterness.

qa.q: What has Gargi learned?
qa.a: To admire people without worshipping them, so that an ordinary flaw doesn't destroy the whole picture.

qa.q: What was Dr Menon actually doing at the conference?
qa.a: Running the whole session: busy, not cold.

grounding: A student who worshipped a mentor turns bitter after one ordinary oversight, then learns to admire without a pedestal.

passage: Department head's note. For a whole term, Arnab treated Dr Sabina as a hero. He sat in the front row, quoted her in every assignment, and told juniors she was "the only real scientist here". Last week she told him his lab report was careless, in front of two others. Since then he has called her "a bully", stopped attending her lab, and asked to change supervisors. I met Arnab today. I agreed the comment could have been made in private. I also asked whether one hard sentence cancels a term of good teaching. He was quiet. We agreed he will meet her with me on Friday before deciding anything.

qa.q: What did Dr Sabina call the lab report?
qa.a: Careless.

qa.q: Why did Arnab swing from calling her a hero to calling her a bully?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and let down by the public criticism, and having put her on a pedestal, one flaw made her seem all bad.

qa.q: How did the department head handle it?
qa.a: Agreed the comment could have been private, asked whether one sentence cancels a term of good teaching, and set up a joint meeting before any decision.

qa.q: How might Dr Sabina feel about Arnab's change?
qa.a: Probably surprised and hurt that one remark led a keen student to call her a bully.

grounding: A student who idolised a professor turns bitter after one harsh comment, and a department head helps him slow down.

passage:
Monday night.
Kishore sent me twelve messages today. For weeks he has said I'm "the only person in this college who gets me", "my real brother". Then last night I missed his call because I was at my cousin's engagement. This morning: "You're useless. You never cared. Everyone's the same." I read it three times, feeling like the floor had tilted. I wanted to reply, "Fine, then find someone else." I didn't. I wrote: "I missed your call because I was at an engagement. I care about you. I'm not okay with being called useless. Let's talk tomorrow after class." Then I put my phone in the drawer. I still feel shaky. But I stayed me.
Jatin

qa.q: Why did Jatin miss Kishore's call?
qa.a: Jatin was at a cousin's engagement.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel reading "You're useless"?
qa.a: Bewildered and shaky, as if the floor had tilted, after weeks of being called a real brother.

qa.q: How did Jatin keep a steady boundary?
qa.a: By explaining the missed call, saying Jatin cares, stating it is not okay to be called useless, suggesting a talk tomorrow, and putting the phone away instead of replying in kind.

qa.q: What might Kishore be feeling when he sends twelve messages?
qa.a: Hurt and abandoned by the missed call, flipping from idealising Jatin to calling Jatin useless.

grounding: A friend once praised as the only one who understands is suddenly called useless after a missed call, and replies with calm boundaries.

passage:
Francis: you're literally the only one who understands me
Francis: seriously, everyone else is fake. you're different
Sahil: haha thanks man 🙂
(two days later)
Francis: where were you?? I called 4 times
Sahil: sorry, was in the lab, phone off
Francis: wow. so you're like the rest. useless
Sahil: that stings. I'm not ignoring you. I was working
Francis: whatever. knew it
Sahil: I get that it felt like I disappeared. that must have been rough
Sahil: but calling me useless isn't fair either
Sahil: I care about you. I'm just not going to argue over text. chai tomorrow at 5, near the library?
Francis: ...fine
Francis: sorry for the useless thing
Sahil: 👍 see you at 5

qa.q: Where was Sahil when Francis called?
qa.a: In the lab, with the phone off.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel on being called useless?
qa.a: Stung and a bit bewildered, after being praised as the only one who understands just two days before.

qa.q: What did Sahil do instead of reacting in kind?
qa.a: Said it stung, acknowledged how the silence felt, named the unfairness calmly, refused to argue over text, and offered chai the next day at 5.

qa.q: What might Francis be feeling behind the word "useless"?
qa.a: Hurt and let down after four unanswered calls, swinging from idealising Sahil to dismissing Sahil.

grounding: A friend idealised as the only one who understands is suddenly called useless after missed calls, and responds with steady boundaries.

passage: In their small town near Mandya, Shalini had spent all summer telling everyone that Chetan was the only person who really understood her. She walked with him to the bus stand every day, shared her poems, called him "my one real friend". Then, on the day of her sister's engagement, he couldn't come because his father's shop needed him. By evening, Shalini had told three people that Chetan was selfish and had never cared. Chetan heard it at the tea stall and felt his stomach drop. He wanted to shout back. Instead he went to her house the next morning. "I couldn't come because of the shop. I'm sorry I missed it. I don't like being called selfish, though. I'd like us to talk properly."

qa.q: Why couldn't Chetan come to the engagement?
qa.a: His father's shop needed him.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel when he heard what Shalini had said?
qa.a: His stomach dropped; he felt hurt and bewildered, and wanted to shout back.

qa.q: How did Chetan keep steady?
qa.a: He went to her calmly, explained, apologised for missing it, said he doesn't like being called selfish, and asked to talk properly.

qa.q: What might Shalini have felt when he didn't come?
qa.a: Deeply let down on an important day, so the hurt flipped her picture of him from perfect to selfish.

grounding: A friend once idealised is suddenly called selfish after missing an event, and responds with calm boundaries instead of anger.

passage: At the dairy cooperative office in Anand, Farhan had noticed a pattern with Sangeeta. Every conflict turned into a story of heroes and villains. Last month the accountant was "the only honest person here". This week, after he questioned her expense slip, he was "a crook who has it in for me". Meanwhile the new clerk who agreed with her was "a saint". Farhan felt uneasy; the office was starting to split. When Sangeeta came in to complain, he didn't take sides. He asked, "What exactly did he say? What happened next?" Slowly the story shrank to one question about a missing receipt. "Let's sort out the receipt," he said, "and I'll talk to him about his tone. You're both valuable here."

qa.q: What did the accountant question?
qa.a: Sangeeta's expense slip.

qa.q: What did Farhan feel about the pattern?
qa.a: Uneasy, because the office was starting to split into heroes and villains.

qa.q: How did Farhan stay fair?
qa.a: He didn't take sides, asked exactly what was said and what happened next, shrank it to the missing receipt, and planned to address the accountant's tone.

qa.q: How might the accountant feel being called a crook?
qa.a: Hurt and unfairly judged, when he had only questioned a receipt.

grounding: A manager notices a staff member sorting colleagues into saints and villains, asks for specifics, and stays fair to all.

passage: In the Nairobi call centre, Nkechi managed eight people, and lately Dalia's reports about the team came in only two colours. "Wanjiru is amazing, she's the only one who works." "Otieno is toxic, he's against me." A week later, after a scheduling clash, Wanjiru became "two-faced". Nkechi noticed her own urge to pick a side, because Dalia told the stories so vividly. Instead, in their one-to-one, she asked, "What exactly happened with the schedule? What did Wanjiru say, word for word?" Dalia hesitated. "She said she couldn't swap shifts." "Anything else?" "No." Nkechi nodded. "So she said no to a swap. That's disappointing. It doesn't make her two-faced." Dalia looked down.

qa.q: What did Wanjiru actually say?
qa.a: That she couldn't swap shifts.

qa.q: What did Nkechi feel pulling at her as Dalia told the stories?
qa.a: A tempted, uneasy urge to take Dalia's side, because the stories were so vivid; she resisted it.

qa.q: How did Nkechi stay fair?
qa.a: She asked what was said, word for word, and named the event as disappointing without labelling Wanjiru.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru feel if she knew she had been called two-faced?
qa.a: Hurt and bewildered, having only declined a shift swap.

grounding: A manager notices a team member sorting colleagues into saints and enemies, asks for specifics, and stays fair to all.

passage: In the staff room of the school where Elizabeth was vice-principal, Abhinav had a new favourite colleague every month. In June it was the music teacher, "a saint". By July, after she took the last projector, she was "selfish, like everyone here". The sports teacher, who had lent him chalk, was now "the only decent person". Elizabeth watched the staff room split into quiet camps. When Abhinav came to her about the projector, she listened and then asked, "Did she know you had booked it?" He paused. "I didn't write it on the sheet." "Okay. So let's fix the booking system." Later she spoke to the music teacher too, so both felt heard. The camps started to soften.

qa.q: What had the sports teacher lent Abhinav?
qa.a: Chalk.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth notice and feel about the staff room?
qa.a: She noticed it splitting into quiet camps and felt concerned.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth stay fair?
qa.a: She listened, asked a specific question about the booking sheet, focused on fixing the system, and spoke to the music teacher too.

qa.q: How might the music teacher feel about being called selfish?
qa.a: Hurt and confused, since she didn't know Abhinav had wanted the projector.

grounding: A vice-principal notices a teacher sorting colleagues into saints and villains, asks for specifics and stays fair to all.
